title: Lab 4
text:
This report describes a lab which uses the STM32L432KC MCU timers to play music given a matrix structure of notes and the number of milliseconds that the notes are played for. This lab took me about 24 hours to complete. This lab meets all of the design specifications listed on the E155 website.

Hardware Specifications
The setup can play a set of musical notes with rests at the correct pitches and for the correct amount of time. It utilizes the 3362P 10K potentiomter to control the volume of the speaker that outputs the music and an LM386 audio amplifier to limit the amount of current that the speaker pulls from the MCU.


Software and Microcontroller Design
This lab uses two timers, timer 6 and timer 7 with custom header files to access all of the registers from memory using structures. An example of the structured register access is included below. All other code can be found in my lab 4 GitHub repository.


Click to view an example of the structured register access for Timer 6





Timer functionality

Timer 6
Timer 6 was used to produce a wave at a specific frequency. This wave was output directly to pin, PB6, which then input that signal into the LM386 audio amplifier, and subsequently the speaker. Timer 6 is driven by the MSI oscillator at 4 MHz, and configured using the PSC prescaler to drive it at 1 MHz. A maxcount value is determined for each desired frequency using the following equation: \[
\mathrm{maxcount} = \frac{1 \mathrm{ MHz}}{f_{des}}
\]
The maxcount is computed as integer division, so any decimal portion will be truncated. This is so that the timer only counts in whole numbers, meaning that it wouldn’t be able to reach the maxcount value if it had decimal numbers in it. Unfortunately, this does produce some error in outputed wave, which is calculated. For example, when the timer is asked to produce a 220 Hz signal, it will have some error: \[
\text{maxcount} = \frac{1 \mathrm{ MHz}}{220 \mathrm{ Hz}} \\
                        = 4545.455 \\
\] Truncated, this gives maxcount = 4545. We can then find the wave this produces by dividing 1 MHz by the 4545, and finding the true frequency of the wave that’s being output. Once that’s done, the error can be found taking the absolute value of the difference between the expected wave frequency and the real wave frequency, all divided by the expected wave frequency: \[
f_{\mathrm{real}} = \frac{1 \mathrm{ MHz}}{4545} \\
                            = 220.022 \mathrm{Hz} \\
\]
\[
\text{percent error} = \frac{220.022 \mathrm{Hz} - 220 \mathrm{Hz}}{220 \mathrm{Hz}}*100\% \\
                         = 0.01 \% \\
\]
This error can be found for each note that is played in Fur Elise. These can be found in the following spreadsheet. All of the errors are highlighted in green, as they have less than 1% error. It is not enough to check that 220 and 1000 Hz have a less than 1% error, because there are values that are higher than 1000 Hz that might cause more error because it is a higher divisor.
The minimum producible frequency is anything between 0 and 1 Hz. This would cause a number that is higher than the highest number that the timer can count to (1,000,000), which would cause the output frequency to be incorrect. The maximum produceable frequency within 1% error is 10,001 Hz, which can be found with this MATLAB code:
    %setup: 
    frequencies = (1:1:1000000); % frequencies to test
    tim_cnt = 1000000; % max number the timer can count to

    % checks for the value where the max freq has >= 1% error
    for i = 1:length(frequencies)
        maxcount = fix(tim_cnt/frequencies(i));
        f_real = tim_cnt/maxcount; 
        error = abs(f_real - frequencies(i))/frequencies(i) * 100; % errror
        if error >= 1
            max_freq = frequencies(i);
            break
        end  
    end 


Timer 7
Timer 7 was used to count the number of seconds for a note (or a rest) to be played. This is essentially like a waiting timer, which counts while timer 6 plays the specific frequency. The timer is driven by the MSI 4 MHz clock, so it has a max count of 4,000,000. Therefore, the minimum number of seconds that it can play for are 0 seconds and it can play for a maximum of 4,000 seconds.


Timer 6 and Timer 7 Interactions
Timer 6 and Timer 7 interact in a simple function called note_and_wait, which calls both of the timer functions and drives the output of timer 6 to the GPIO pin.


Click to view note_and_wait






Schematic
The schematic for the speaker is included below: 


AI Prototype
I used Gemini, which was fairly helpful. It chose a different timer than I did, stating that TIM2 would be the best choice. It chose that because it knew all of the information and setup steps in order to configure timer 2 to best work and because timer 2 can directly drive a GPIO output, while I wanted to use TIM6 and TIM7 because they were easier for me to understand. It told explained almost all of the correct registers to enable, however it recommended using an 80MHz PLL to drive the timer, but 1) didn’t explain how to configure the PLL and 2) ended up dividing by 80 using the prescaler inside the timer, so it seemed like an odd choice to use PLL. As the answers were all correct, I didn’t feel the need to attach the reference manual.
I think that the most useful thing it could do was find all the steps to configure all the specific registers, because it is easy to miss a couple steps when doing the lab, which will cause the entire system not to work. However, because it also missed some steps and made some questionable decisions, that could cause more work (like using the PLL), I think that it is still useful to look in the reference manual yourself to at least get a tentative idea of the different functionalities.

title: Lab 1
text:
This report describes the FPGA and MCU Verifcation lab, lab 1. This lab took me about 32 hours to complete. Future versions of this lab should look at what is necessary for completing the lab (i.e. if multiple Git tutorials, which are actually helpful), so as to avoid overwhelming students with many extra tutorials that weren’t necessarily helpful to the current lab.

Hardware Specifications
The development board is fully assembled. It is able to display all sixteen hexadecimal numbers. The image below shows the digit F. The dipswitches are arranged for the seven-segment so that when all the switches are closest to the FPGA, the output on the seven-segment display is zero. The rightmost digit is bit 0 and the leftmost digit is bit 1.


Click to view dipswitches and seven-segment display

 Dipswitches
 Seven-segment display

The LEDs have the specified logic operations. The picture below shows the case where both LED 0 and 1 are on, LED 2 is blinking.


Click to view LEDs



The FPGA is coded with Verilog code through the use of modules.


Click to view top level module





Verilog Structure and Style
The FPGA was coded with three Verilog Modules. lab1_kl is the top-level module with assign statements for LED[1] and LED[0], led_blinker controls the blinking LED (LED[2]) through a counter, and display_led controls the seven-segment display connected to the board.


Click to view lab1_kl





Click to view led_blinker





Click to view display_led





Simulations and Waveforms
Questa was used for simulations with testbenches for all modules.
The first module is the main testbench. The waveform shows that the LEDs l and 2 are on when the correct s-signals are on.


Click to view LED[1] and LED[0] waveforms



The second module is the blinker module. The four figures below show the reset and counter resetting functionality.


Click to view LED[2] waveforms

 Reset = 1, enable = 1, LED is on
 Reset = 1, enable = 0, LED is off
 Reset = 0, enable = 1, LED is off
 Reset = 0, enable = 0, LED is off

The third module is the seven segment-module, which matches the 15 states that the DIP switch (controlled by s) can be in.


Click to view seven-segment waveforms





Schematic and Block Diagram Specs
The first schematic shows how the seven-segment LED is powered and run from the Upduino.


Click to view LED Schematics – LED[2:0] and seven-segment LEDs.



The second schematic shows the different digital modules created inside of verilog.


Click to view LED Schematics – LED[2:0] and seven-segment LEDs.





Calculations
The seven-segment led requires pulldown resistors connected to ground, which need to be calculated based on the amount of voltage that the LED takes and the desired current through the pin and LEDs.


Click to view resistor calculations.



Additionally, in order to make a counter that took a 24MHz signal and take it down to a 2.4 Hz signal, calculations were neeed.


Click to view clock counter calculations





AI Prototype
I used Gemini for my AI Prototype. After a input the initial code, there were three errors. First, one error was because there was no top-level specified module, which was my fault because this is something you need to set in Radiant rather than through the code. The second was that Gemini used an outdated version to reference the high-speed oscillator, which Radiant didn’t recognize. Finally, in its configuration of the high-speed oscillator, the AI set the oscillator to 48 MHz when it said it was setting it to 12 MHz. Without having done this lab on my own, I might not have known that and I would’ve been confused as to why it didn’t work. The AI did add some useful lines of code, however. Instead of parameterizing the module, it used local parameters to define the max count and the width. It also used the $clog2, which is a built-in function that calculates the minumum number of bits needed to make the argument of the function, which seems like it would be useful (see below).

If I were to use an LLM in my workflow further, I would ask it questions about errors and feed it the code that was causing the errors, because the LLM was able to address the errors when confronted about them.

title: Lab 2
text:
This report describes a lab which uses one seven-segment SystemVerilog module to light up a double seven-segment display, by alternating between lighting them at 100Hz (faster than the human eye can detect). The lab also includes a scanner for a keypad, where signals are put through each of the rows and if a column is pressed, an LED lights up. This lab took me about 18 hours to complete. One thing that would help a future version of this lab is a better diagram or explanation of how the scanner for the keypad is working, because the current figure seems misleading.

Hardware Specifications
The FPGA pins are in series with resistors from Radiant, which are 100K. The scanning signals appear in each of the columns when the LEDs are pressed, working even when multiple buttons in the same column or the same row are pressed.


Verilog Structure and Style
This lab was done in two separate LatticeRadiant build projects. The counter module uses the same code between projects, so it is only displayed once. The first project is the seven-segment decoder, which only includes a single seven-segment module that is time multiplexed.


Click to view top-level seven-segment module


Includes: HSOSC, one seven-seg module, multiplexed counter module, and assign statments to implement multiplexing.



Click to view seven-seg module


This was used in Lab 1, with updates made to the code for Lab 2.



Click to view the mux module





Click to view counter module



The second project is the keypad project which scans through the rows of the keypad.


Click to view top-level keypad module


Includes: scanning module (my module name: keypad), and assign statments to light up the LEDs based on the column outputs.



Click to view scanning module


Includes: counter and assign statements. The counter is resettable and enable-able, therefore, so is the scanning module.



Simulations and Waveforms
Questa was used for simulations with testbenches for all new modules.
The first waveform is for the seven-segment LED showing the multiplexing functionality of the module. The waveform shows that when s changes, chosen_dip changes between dip1 and dip2 (the two switches that send the signals to the two different seven-segment displays).


Click to view dip1, dip2, and chosen_dip waveforms



The second set of waveforms is for the scanning module. The first attacment demonstrates that the rows alternate, while the second two attachments display the reset and enable features.


Click to view alternating row waveforms





Click to view reset and enable features for the counting module in waveforms


This is the reset feature. When reset is pressed, the row signal returns to its default state, jumping from 0100 to 0001.

This is the enable feature. When enable is pressed, the row signal holds the current signal it was at when enable was pressed until enable is let go.

The final set of waveforms is from the top module of the keypad project. The following four attachments demonstrate the LED driving functionality of the top module.


Click to view LED waveforms

 LED[0] is on
 LED[1] is on
 LED[2] is on
 LED[3] is on



Block Diagram and Schematic Specs
The first block diagram is for the first project (double seven-segment LED).


Click to view the first block diagram



The second block diagram displays the second project (the keypad).



Click to view the second block diagram



The first schematic is for the first project (double seven-segment LED).


Click to view the first block schematic



The second schematic displays the second project (the keypad).



Click to view the second block diagram





Calculations
The first schematic shows how the FPGA pins are in the reccomended operating ranges (calculation done for the FPGA pin connected to the PNP transistor connected to the seven-segment LED).


Click to view FPGA pin calculation for the seven-segment diagram

 PNP to anode turning on pin calculation.
 PNP to seven-segment LED pin calculation.



Click to view FPGA pin calculation for the seven-segment diagram

 PNP to keypad row pin.



AI Prototype
My reflection on the outcome of this might be fairly standard. The output was better when given the extra file and info. Therefore, when coding using an LLM, it might be helpful to give it as much information as possible, so that it can work within your constraints better. I think the one downside of this is that it doesn’t allow the LLM as much ingenuity. For example, if you specified a constraint of using combinational logic in a certain case, but the LLM actually has seen a use-case of something else that implements your desired design better, then you would probably want to see that.

title: Blog posts
text: My goal in this class is to work towards a better understanding of microprocessors and the sensors that they countrol. I have concentrated my work at Mudd in biomedical research, projects, and classes, and I hope to apply microps to that area. Sensors are integral to the biomedical field and learning how to implement them with a microcontroller is something that I hope to do for my final project as well as further on in my career.
